To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) exercise training is effective in reducing blood pressure in older adults, 2) the effect of exercise training on blood pressure is independent of age, gender, and initial blood pressure, 3) the reduction in systolic and diastolic blood pressure is comparable to that achieved with antihypertensive drug therapy, and 4) the effect of aerobic exercise is comparable to that of resistance training, and 5) the effect is independent of the mode of exercise. 1

(a) exercise is a safe and effective way to lower blood pressure, especially in people who are overweight or obese; and (b) exercise can be as beneficial as medication, but it is not as effective as medication plus exercise.
The effect of exercise on blood pressures was modest, but the effects of the interventions were similar in magnitude to those of other non-pharmacological interventions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of exercise on blood pressures in older persons.
the effects of exercise on blood pressures.
the effects of physical activity, exercise, and fitness on cardiovascular disease and risk factors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
exercise training is effective in reducing blood pressure in hypertensive patients, but the effect is modest and not as large as pharmacological treatment.
exercise is an effective treatment for high blood pressure.
exercise has a positive effect on BP and is recommended in the treatment of hypertension in older persons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the results are consistent with a causal relationship between physical activity and blood pressure reduction in adults, but that the relationship is complex and the evidence is mixed, with some studies showing a benefit and some not.
the effect of exercise training on blood pressure (BP) is not as strong as the effect on cardiovascular risk factors.
the effect of exercise on blood-pressure is modest and may be influenced by the type and amount of exercise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of exercise on blood sugar control is not a one-size-fits-all proposition.
exercise can reduce blood pressure in people with hypertension and that it can also reduce blood pressure in those who don’t have hypertension.
the effects of exercise on BP are not uniform across the population and that exercise may have differential effects depending on the initial BP of the individual.
